newsitem.title: USA: Strong November spending presages merry Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Strong November spending presages merry Christmas.

text.p: Consumers earned more and spent more in November, the government said Monday, helping the important holiday shopping season get off to a solid start.

With about half of all retail sales usually coming in the few weeks from Thanksgiving through Christmas, the Commerce Department said November spending rose 0.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.24 trillion.
That followed a revised 0.7 percent gain in October, which was the strongest since a 0.8 percent rise in May, the department said. It previously reported that spending rose 0.5 percent in October.

Analysts said the solid rise in spending in the two months, together with a rebound in incomes in November augured well for the holiday season and for the economy heading into 1997. Retailers can earn a quarter or more of their annual profits during the holiday selling season.
"The spending increase is fairly consistent with modest but healthy holiday sales that we are beginning to see right now," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.
Good job prospects and rising incomes have bolstered consumer confidence heading into the new year, Sohn said, providing a solid base for the 5-1/2-year-old economic expansion to continue next year.
The department said incomes rose 0.5 percent last month to an annual rate of $6.57 trillion after being unchanged in October.

Separately, Cahners Economics Inc. of Newton, Mass., said its latest survey of 400 senior business executives found them upbeat about next year with 71 percent describing current business conditions as good to excellent.
Its Cahners Business Confidence Index, which measures seven indicators from employment to production to research and development spending, rose to 66.2 in December from 65.2 in November.
The government report on rising November earnings and spending had been expected because of previous reports of strong job creation and higher earnings last month.

The department said wages and salaries grew $22.5 billion in November after dropping $4.9 billion in October. Gains in personal income tend to help boost consumer spending, which fuels about two-thirds of economic activity.
Consumers saved 5 cents out of each dollar earned last month, unchanged from October, the report said.
Sohn of Norwest Corp. said last month's steady savings rate suggested consumers were continuing efforts to balance their household finances and bring credit card payments under control.
Last week, the American Bankers Association said late payments on credit cards fell to a seasonally adjusted 3.48 percent in the third quarter from a record 3.66 percent in the second quarter.

"This is an attempt by consumers to rebalance and get their financial houses in order," Sohn said, which should contribute to modest economic growth of 2.5 percent to 3 percent in the fourth quarter, up from the 2.1 percent pace registered in the third quarter.
"It's moderate but healthy economic growth," Sohn said.
A separate University of Michigan consumer confidence survey, issued Monday to paying subscribers, showed a drop in December to a reading of 96.9 from 99.2 in November.

But Jean Sundrla, a currency analyst with MCM MoneyWatch in New York, said the November index was inflated by "election euphoria" as politicians on the stump stressed positive issues ahead of Nov. 5, election day.
"Sentiment itself remains fairly strong," Sundrla said noting media reports indicate retailers are doing "quite well."
Spending on durable goods, which includes cars, furniture and other items intended to last three years or more, rose 0.6 percent in November to an annual rate of $637 billion.
Spending on non-durable products rose 0.2 percent to a rate of $1.56 trillion. Spending for services edged up 0.7 percent to $3.04 trillion.
